title: Investigation Guide
intro: Short recipes for the questions most investigations start with: where the answer is recorded, which Kairon view shows it, and searches to run.

topics.question: What ran on the host?
topics.why: Program execution is the backbone of most investigations: it tells you which tools the intruder used and when.

searches.label: Process creation in the Security log (4688)
Sysmon process creation, with command line and hashes
Anything run from a user's Temp folder

sources.name: Prefetch
sources.detail: C:\Windows\Prefetch: last run times and run count

sources.name: Amcache
sources.detail: Amcache.hve: path and SHA-1 of executables seen

sources.name: Shimcache
sources.detail: AppCompatCache in SYSTEM: presence and order

sources.name: Security 4688
sources.detail: process creation, when auditing is enabled

sources.name: Sysmon 1
sources.detail: process creation with command line, parent and hashes

look_for: Binaries in AppData, Temp, ProgramData or Downloads
Names that imitate system tools (scvhost.exe, lsas.exe)
Office or browsers starting cmd.exe or powershell.exe

topics.question: How does it survive a reboot?
topics.why: Persistence is how an intruder keeps access; finding it tells you what to clean and often when the compromise began.

sources.name: Run / RunOnce
sources.detail: HKLM and HKCU \Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run

sources.name: Services
sources.detail: System 7045 and Security 4697 when a service is installed

sources.name: Scheduled tasks
sources.detail: Security 4698, Task Scheduler 106, C:\Windows\System32\Tasks

sources.name: WMI subscriptions
sources.detail: WMI-Activity 5861

sources.name: Startup folders
sources.detail: the Start Menu Startup folders of every user

look_for: Services or tasks pointing at user folders or script interpreters
Random-looking names or descriptions
Anything created shortly before the first suspicious activity

topics.question: Who logged on, and from where?
topics.why: Logons tie activity to an account and a source address, and show password guessing that eventually worked.

searches.label: Accounts created or added to a group

sources.detail: successful and failed logons; the logon type says how (2 keyboard, 3 network, 10 RDP)
logon with explicit credentials (runas, lateral movement tools)
administrative privileges assigned at logon
account created / user added to a local group

look_for: Many 4625 followed by a 4624 from the same address
Logons at unusual hours
Accounts created and used shortly after

topics.question: Did it move to other machines?
topics.why: Lateral movement turns one compromised host into many; it decides the scope of the investigation.

sources.name: Remote Desktop
sources.detail: 4624 type 10 and the RDP connection logs

sources.name: Admin shares
sources.detail: 5140 / 5145 for ADMIN$ and C$

sources.name: PsExec and clones
sources.detail: a new PSEXESVC (or similar) service, 7045

sources.name: WinRM
sources.detail: wsmprovhost.exe running commands

look_for: The same account logging on to several hosts in a short time
A service installed right after a network logon from another host

topics.question: What did PowerShell do?
topics.why: PowerShell is the most common tool for intruders on Windows; script block logging often records the whole payload.

sources.name: PowerShell Operational
sources.detail: 4104 script blocks, 4103 module logging

sources.name: Windows PowerShell
sources.detail: 800 pipeline execution

sources.name: PSReadLine
sources.detail: ConsoleHost_history.txt of every user

look_for: -enc / -EncodedCommand
DownloadString, Invoke-WebRequest, IEX
Execution policy bypass, AMSI tampering

topics.question: Which files and folders were opened?
topics.why: File opening shows what the user (or intruder) looked at or staged before taking it.

sources.name: LNK
sources.detail: the Recent folder: target path, volume and times

sources.name: Jump Lists
sources.detail: recent items per application

sources.name: ShellBags
sources.detail: folders browsed, including on removable drives and shares

sources.name: RecentDocs / OpenSaveMRU
sources.detail: files opened or saved per user

look_for: Archives or documents opened from USB drives or network shares
Folders browsed on other hosts

topics.question: Where did it come from?
topics.why: The way in (a download, an e-mail attachment) tells you what else may have been sent and to whom.

searches.label: Files downloaded from the internet (Mark of the Web)

sources.name: Browser history
sources.detail: visited URLs and downloads

sources.name: Zone.Identifier
sources.detail: Mark of the Web stream with the source URL

sources.name: E-mail
sources.detail: attachments and links

sources.name: Office
sources.detail: trust records and alerts when macros were enabled

look_for: Executables, scripts, ISO or archive files downloaded shortly before the first execution
Documents whose macros were enabled

topics.question: Were USB devices used?
topics.why: USB devices can bring malware in or take data out.

sources.name: setupapi.dev.log
sources.detail: first connection of each device

sources.name: USBSTOR / MountedDevices
sources.detail: SYSTEM hive: device, serial, drive letter

sources.name: Partition/Diagnostic
sources.detail: connection events with volume details

look_for: Devices first seen during the incident window
LNK files pointing at removable drives

topics.question: What was deleted?
topics.why: Deletion often follows staging or covers tracks; the file system remembers more than the Recycle Bin.

sources.name: MFT
sources.detail: every file record, including deleted ones

sources.name: USN Journal
sources.detail: create, rename and delete operations

sources.name: Recycle Bin
sources.detail: $I files with the original path and deletion time

look_for: Tools and archives deleted after use
Mass renames (ransomware)

topics.question: Were the tracks covered?
topics.why: Cleared logs and disabled defences are strong signs of hands-on-keyboard activity.

sources.detail: Security / System log cleared (provider Microsoft-Windows-Eventlog)

sources.name: Defender
sources.detail: 1116/1117 detections, 5001 real-time protection disabled
audit policy changed

look_for: Log clearing shortly after suspicious logons
Defender disabled or exclusions added

topics.question: What did it connect to?
topics.why: Outbound connections reveal command-and-control servers and exfiltration.

sources.name: Sysmon 3 / 22
sources.detail: network connections and DNS queries per process

sources.name: Windows Firewall log
sources.detail: allowed and dropped connections

look_for: Rare domains or direct connections to IP addresses
Scripting engines or Office making network connections

topics.question: Who logged in, and who tried?
topics.why: On Linux, SSH logins and failures are the most common way in, and brute force leaves a clear trail.

sources.name: auth.log / secure
sources.detail: SSH, sudo and su

sources.name: wtmp / btmp
sources.detail: logins and reboots / failed logins, with exact times

sources.name: lastlog
sources.detail: last login of every account

look_for: Bursts of failures from one address followed by a success
Logins as root
Accounts that never log in suddenly doing so

topics.question: What was run as root?
topics.why: sudo and su show which account became root and what it ran.

sources.name: auth.log
sources.detail: sudo lines: user, target account, directory and command

sources.name: sudoers
sources.detail: who may run what as whom

look_for: Service accounts (www-data, mail) using sudo
sudo to a shell (sudo -i, sudo su -)

topics.question: How does it survive a reboot?
topics.why: Cron jobs, systemd units, preloaded libraries and SSH keys are the usual ways to keep access on Linux.

searches.label: Flagged persistence (download-and-run, reverse shells, preloads, PAM)
searches.query: artifact:linux_persistence AND (indicator:download_and_run OR indicator:reverse_shell OR indicator:obfuscation OR indicator:preload_library OR indicator:pam_exec OR indicator:auth_always_permit OR indicator:shadowed_command_alias)

sources.name: cron
sources.detail: /etc/crontab, /etc/cron.*, /var/spool/cron

sources.name: systemd
sources.detail: unit files

sources.name: rc.local, ld.so.preload, PAM
sources.detail: boot scripts, preloaded libraries, authentication modules

sources.name: Shell start-up
sources.detail: .bashrc, /etc/profile.d

sources.name: SSH
sources.detail: authorized_keys

look_for: Jobs running from /tmp, /dev/shm or hidden folders
curl … | sh
Keys in authorized_keys nobody can explain

topics.question: What commands were typed?
topics.why: Shell history is often the most direct record of what an intruder did.

searches.label: curl, netcat, base64
searches.query: artifact:linux_shell_history AND (command:*curl* OR command:*nc* OR command:*base64*)

sources.name: .bash_history / .zsh_history
sources.detail: commands per user, usually without times

sources.name: auditd
sources.detail: execve records when the audit daemon runs

look_for: Downloads, permission changes (chmod +x), history clearing
Commands run from /tmp

topics.question: Was the web server attacked?
topics.why: Web applications are a frequent way in; decoded requests show payloads and reverse shells.

sources.name: access.log / error.log
sources.detail: Apache and nginx; requests are decoded and flagged with what they contain

look_for: Requests to unusual scripts (web shells)
An address and port in a request (reverse shell)
Errors right before a new process or account

topics.question: What was installed?
topics.why: Installed packages show tools brought in by the intruder (scanners, compilers, netcat).

sources.name: dpkg.log, apt history.log
sources.detail: Debian/Ubuntu

sources.name: yum.log, dnf.log
sources.detail: Red Hat family

look_for: Tools installed during the incident window

topics.question: Which accounts exist?
topics.why: New or altered accounts are a common way to keep access.

sources.name: /etc/passwd, /etc/group
sources.detail: accounts and groups

sources.name: /etc/shadow
sources.detail: only whether a password is set; hashes are never stored

look_for: A second account with UID 0
Service accounts with a login shell
New members of sudo or wheel

topics.question: Can the times be trusted?
topics.why: Syslog lines have no year and most logs have no time zone; Kairon converts them, and says how.

searches.label: Lines whose year or zone was inferred
searches.query: timequality:inferred_year_host_timezone OR timequality:inferred_year OR timequality:assumed_year_utc OR timequality:assumed_utc

sources.name: Time Quality column
sources.detail: how each line's time was obtained

look_for: Check a line's time quality before relying on its exact time
